subtitulo: Cutting who and which out of your descriptions
descripcion: This is a structural difference between B2 and C1 written English. *The patients who were given the drug* becomes *the patients given the drug*. The information is identical; the density is not. The rule is narrow and learnable: drop the relative pronoun and the auxiliary when the clause is passive or continuous, and only when the pronoun is the **subject**.

ejemplos.texto: *The study, published last month, contradicts three earlier trials.*
*Anyone taking that medication should avoid alcohol.*
*Having been misdiagnosed twice, she stopped trusting the referral system.*
*Weighed against the side effects, the benefit looks smaller.*
*The data available doesn't support that conclusion.*

notas: Present participle = active; past participle = passive. Getting this backwards is the classic error.
Dangling participles are common and real: the participle's subject must be the main clause's subject.
These are written structures. In conversation they sound stiff.

es.en: Spanish has gerund and participle clauses too, but tolerates a dangling subject far more readily (estando en Madrid, me robaron). English does not: the same construction reads as an error.
es.es: El español también tiene cláusulas de gerundio y participio, pero tolera mucho más fácilmente un sujeto colgante («estando en Madrid, me robaron»). El inglés no: la misma construcción se lee como un error.

de.en: German compresses relative clauses into participles placed before the noun (die mit dem Medikament behandelten Patienten), while English places them after it (the patients given the drug). German speakers therefore know the compression but have to move the whole participle phrase behind the noun.
de.de: Deutsch verdichtet Relativsätze zu Partizipgruppen vor dem Substantiv («die mit dem Medikament behandelten Patienten»), während Englisch sie danach stellt («the patients given the drug»). Deutschsprachige kennen also die Verdichtung, müssen aber die gesamte Partizipgruppe hinter das Substantiv verschieben.

it.en: Reduced relatives are easy, because Italian uses exactly the same postnominal participle (i pazienti trattati con il farmaco – the patients treated with the drug). The risk lies in participle and gerund clauses: colloquial Italian tolerates a different subject (essendo a Madrid, mi hanno derubato), while English treats this as an error.
it.it: Le relative ridotte sono facili, perché l'italiano usa esattamente lo stesso participio postnominale («i pazienti trattati con il farmaco» – «the patients treated with the drug»). Il rischio sta nelle clausole participiali e gerundive: l'italiano colloquiale tollera più facilmente un soggetto diverso («essendo a Madrid, mi hanno derubato»), mentre l'inglese lo considera un errore.

fr.en: Reduced relatives are easy, since French uses the same postnominal participle (les patients traités avec le médicament). French school grammar also insists that the gérondif shares the subject of the main clause, so French speakers already know the rule that prevents dangling participles in English.
fr.fr: Les relatives réduites sont faciles, car le français utilise le même participe postposé («les patients traités avec le médicament»). La grammaire scolaire française insiste aussi sur le fait que le gérondif partage le sujet de la proposition principale, donc les francophones connaissent déjà la règle qui évite les dangling participles en anglais.

pt.en: Reduced relatives are easy, since Portuguese uses the same postnominal participle (os doentes tratados com o fármaco). Gerund clauses with a different subject are common, especially in Brazilian Portuguese, so dangling participles are the main risk.
pt.pt: As relativas reduzidas são fáceis, pois o português usa o mesmo particípio depois do substantivo («os doentes tratados com o fármaco»). Orações de gerúndio com sujeito diferente são comuns, sobretudo no português brasileiro, então dangling participles são o principal risco.

errores: *Walking into the room, the lights were off* — the lights were not walking.
Reducing where the pronoun is the object: *the book read*.

es: Copying the Spanish gerund of posteriority: *He resigned in May, being replaced in June* instead of *and was replaced in June*.
de: Placing the participle and its complements before the noun: *the in 2019 built plant* instead of *the plant built in 2019*.
it: Copying the Italian absolute participle: *Finished the work, we left* from *finito il lavoro* instead of *Having finished the work, we left*.
fr: Copying *une fois le travail terminé*: *Once the work finished, we left* instead of *Once the work was finished*.
pt: Copying the gerund of posteriority: *The company closed in 2020, leaving the market in 2021* for two separate events instead of *and left the market in 2021*.

vocabulario.item: to get the hang of something

traducciones.es: una escapada de fin de semana
traducciones.pt: uma escapadinha de fim de semana

mision.consigna: Write a profile of a hobby you've tried, for a club newsletter aimed at complete beginners.
requisitos: five reduced relatives or participle clauses
at least one case where you keep the full relative on purpose, because the pronoun is an object
use *spare time*, *to take up a hobby* and *to get the hang of something*

microtareas.texto: Write five sentences with *who is / which was*, then cut them down. Which ones can't be cut?
Describe people at your gym or club: *anyone taking…*, *the ones given…*. Five lines.
Record 90 seconds: what helps you *unwind* after work? Use two participle clauses.

autochequeo: Active or passive participle — the right one in each case?
Is the participle's subject the same as the main clause's?
Did I reduce any object-pronoun clause illegally?
Is the text still readable, or just dense?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on reduced relative and participle clauses. (1) Check active vs passive in each. (2) Flag every dangling participle and show the fix. (3) Flag reductions that are not grammatically allowed. (4) Say whether the density is helping or hurting readability. Do not rewrite the text.
